summary: Specifies an architecture and gateway-to-gateway protocol to provide Fibre Channel fabric functionality over an IP network. It uses TCP for Fibre Channel frame transport and supports the Fibre Channel distributed fabric services. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Fibre Channel storage devices can communicate across an Internet Protocol (IP) network through iFCP gateways. The gateways discover remote devices, carry their frames over Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), and handle addressing so the devices can keep using Fibre Channel.

subtitle: Gateways that carry Fibre Channel storage frames between regions over TCP/IP.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel storage traffic uses its own fabric and address system. Connecting separate regions over an IP network requires gateways that preserve the devices' expected fabric behavior.
tldr.mechanism: iFCP gateways discover remote ports through iSNS, establish TCP connections between port pairs, and encapsulate Fibre Channel frames for transport over IP.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines address-translation and address-transparent modes. RFC 4172 was later updated by RFC 6172 and RFC 7146.

sections.title: What iFCP Provides
sections.content:
The Internet Fibre Channel Protocol (iFCP) is a gateway-to-gateway protocol that provides Fibre Channel fabric services to Fibre Channel devices over Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP). It uses TCP for congestion control, error detection, and recovery while carrying Fibre Channel frames between remote ports.

The gateways pass ordinary frame traffic and emulate fabric services where needed. The RFC identifies the mapping between Fibre Channel and TCP/IP, especially its protocol section, as the authoritative part of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Fibre Channel devices can send frames through gateways across an Internet Protocol (IP) network. The gateway carries the frames and presents the fabric behavior the devices expect.

sections.title: Gateway Regions and iSNS
sections.content:
Each iFCP gateway connects a local Fibre Channel region to the IP network. To devices inside its region, the gateway appears as a Fibre Channel switch; on the IP side, it represents local ports as logical Fibre Channel devices.

The Internet Storage Name Service (iSNS) supports discovery and configuration. Gateways use it to find remote ports, organize gateways into fabrics, apply discovery domains, and distribute security policies. Access to an iSNS server is required.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway represents its local storage devices to remote gateways. iSNS acts as the directory that helps gateways discover ports and organize the storage network.

sections.title: Two Addressing Modes
sections.content:
In address-translation mode, an address is local to a gateway region. A gateway assigns an alias to each remote port; when a frame arrives, it fills in the destination port address and the alias, then recalculates the Fibre Channel CRC. This mode supports unbounded fabrics and MUST be supported.

In address-transparent mode, addresses are unique across a bounded fabric and no translation occurs. The iSNS server allocates domain IDs, and the combined number of gateways and switch elements is limited by the Fibre Channel address space. Support for this mode is OPTIONAL.
sections.plainLanguage: One mode gives each gateway region local addresses and translates remote addresses as frames arrive. The other uses unique addresses across the whole fabric and does not translate them, but has a size limit.

sections.title: Sessions Between Fibre Channel Ports
sections.content:
An iFCP session connects a pair of N_PORTs with one TCP connection. No more than one session may exist for a given pair. A gateway locates the remote port, allocates a TCP connection, sends a CBIND message, and waits for a successful response before sending Fibre Channel frames.

A session can be OPEN PENDING or OPEN. Gateways may send LTEST messages to check whether a connection is live, and UNBIND messages to end a session. Gateways can also keep unused TCP connections in a pool for later session setup.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ports communicate through a TCP connection assigned to that pair. The gateways bind the connection before sending frames and can test whether it remains active.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The RFC relies on IPsec for confidentiality, authentication, integrity, and replay protection, and requires support for IKE key management. It describes threats including snooping, packet modification, injection, connection hijacking, denial of service, and attacks on iSNS communication.

RFC 4172 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 6172 and RFC 7146. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.
sections.plainLanguage: Because iFCP traffic crosses an IP network, the RFC specifies IPsec and key-management requirements to protect it. RFC 6172 and RFC 7146 later updated this Proposed Standard.
